subtopic: NAVY, ARMY AND AIR FORCE OFFICER TRAINING AT ROYAL ROADS AND ROYAL MILITARY COLLEGE

speakeroldname: Hon. BROOKE CLAXTON (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: NAVY, ARMY AND AIR FORCE OFFICER TRAINING AT ROYAL ROADS AND ROYAL MILITARY COLLEGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe it would be the wish of hon. members that I should make a statement drawing to the attention of the house and the country the
arrangements made for the training of officers for the Royal Canadian Navy, the Canadian Army and the Royal Canadian Air Force.
During the war, combined operations under unified command brought victory to the allied side. Considerable progress has already been made in the unification of the Department of National Defence and in the co-ordination of the three services.
As a beginning in co-operation we have decided to require the same entrance qualification and to give the same general education at the same places for cadets in all three services. This arrangement has been worked out after studies of educational experience in this country as well as in Great Britain, the United States, Australia and elsewhere.
The naval college at Royal Roads was this year extended to include air cadets. In September it will also be open to candidates for the army. Royal Roads will have a two-year course, corresponding closely to the first two years in engineering at a university.
Also in September of this year Royal Military College, Kingston, will reopen for cadets for the three services. The first two years will be identical with those at Royal Roads and there will be a further two years, making a four-year course in all. On the completion of their course at Royal Roads cadets for all branches of the three services will go on to complete their course at Royal Military College except that cadets for the executive and marine engineering branches of the navy, after two years at Royal Military College o? Royal Roads, will take special training before being posted as sub-lieutenants.
Entrance requirements for both Royal Roads and Royal Military College will be senior matriculation or its equivalent. Candidates must have reached their sixteenth but not their twentieth birthday on 1st January preceding entrance. Naval applicants, except in the case of candidates from classical colleges, must not have reached their nineteenth birthday on 1st January.
The standard achieved will be approximately the same as that in a four-years arts course and three years towards an engineering degree. Following graduation from Royal Military College, students in technical and engineering subjects will be carried on for an extra year at a university to give them a university degree.
National Defence

During the summer months students will do three and half months' practical work with their branch of their service. At the end of the course they will thus have completed almost a year's practical training in addition to their general education, which will be on a broader basis than ever before.
The second source of officers is the universities. Arrangements have been made with twenty-two universities under which undergraduates may join the Canadian officers' training corps or university naval training division. Under these arrangements, students will receive theoretical training during the college term and will spend three and a half months in the summer doing practical work together with the cadets from Royal Roads and Royal Military College. At the completion of their university courses, in addition to their degree, they will have had additional theoretical military work and the equivalent of a year's practical training with their service. Similar arrangements are in effect for the air force.
Under all these plans, the pay received during the summer months will make a substantial contribution towards the cost of tuition and other expenses during the college term.
The third source of officer material is in promotion from the ranks. It is hoped that as many as twenty per cent of officers will be selected in this way. Officer cadets from the ranks will attend either one of the Canada service colleges or the universities at government expense.
These arrangements for officer training are in addition to service schools for training in the use of weapons and trades schools in all three services. A number of schools are of an inter-service nature, such as the joint army-air school at Rivers, where all aspects of army-air force co-operation are studied, or the winter warfare school at Churchill, where all three services and the defence research board are studying techniques of winter warfare. There are as well army and air staff colleges, and the national defence college for senior officers and civilian officials opened at Kingston on the 5th January last.
Further, all three services have specialist officers undergoing post-graduate training at universities in Canada.
Another educational scheme of importance is the institution of language training. The army is putting into effect French classes in every command and training centre. At headquarters 178 officers are taking voluntary courses in French. Provision is also made for training in languages other than French. The navy and air force will soon implement similar plans.

Modern war requires technical abilities of the highest order. Should an emergency arise, the outcome may well turn on the professional skills and qualities of leadership of the staffs and fighting formations of every branch of every service. For this reason we are trying to ensure that the Canadian defence forces will be led by men who will live up to the fighting reputation of Canadians and who will also have the intelligence and knowledge to develop and use the weapons and skills that may be necessary for the effective defence of our country.

subtopic: MOVEMENT OF NOVA SCOTIA RESIDENTS TO EMPLOYMENT ELSEWHERE

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: MOVEMENT OF NOVA SCOTIA RESIDENTS TO EMPLOYMENT ELSEWHERE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) asked me to give details of the movement of residents of Nova Scotia to work elsewhere in Canada.
A group movement plan was authorized in January 1947, but most of the new placements were in the autumn months of that year. The total, men and women, was 2.642, of which 2,354 were men. Of these, 1,627 were transferred from Sydney, 341 from New Glasgow, 183 from Halifax, 175 from Amherst, 16 from Yarmouth, 6 from Bridgewater and 6 from Liverpool.
Through the national employment service, 254 went to gold and base metal mines in northern Ontario, 211 to a nickel refinery, 761 to farm implement plants; and the remainder were absorbed by foundries, paper mills, textile mills, other manufacturing and construction.
Of the 288 women and girls transferred, 257 came from Sydney, 27 from New Glasgow -and 4 from Amherst. They found work in shoe, textile, rubber, and food processing plants. Under this plan transportation and medical examination costs were paid by the federal government.
In addition, jobs were found for residents of the maritimes individually. It is estimated 1,200 men and women were thus referred to vacancies offered by employers elsewhere during 1947.
There were other organized movements, largely confined to the east, with transportation paid by employers and workers.
In the potato picking season, 600 New Brunswick residents were found jobs in Maine and 700 Nova Scotians were found jobs in
Prince Edward Island. For apple picking, 1,500 Nova Scotians were registered and found jobs in the Annapolis valley; 200 New Brunswick residents were transferred to pea vining operations in Maine. More than 400 woods workers were transferred from New Brunswick to Maine. This is a total of more than 3,400.

speechtext: Replying to the general question which my hon. friend has put, as to whether consultation was had with outside interests to find out what should be included in the prohibited list and what should not, the answer is no, for reasons which all members of the committee will appreciate. Advance discussion was not possible. In selecting the articles which were to be included in schedule I, the prohibited list, or schedule II, the quota list, exhaustive study was given to trade statistics and production statistics in Canada, import records, and all that sort of thing, by an inter-departmental committee headed by Mr. Taylor, to which I referred a few days ago. Speaking generally, where things on the prohibited list are in the category of necessities or desirable items, they would not be put there unless it was felt that the source of supply in Canada was reasonably adequate. I think that would apply to flashlights, which were mentioned by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie. I think there is fairly adequate production of flashlights in Canada. I am speaking from memory in discussing the schedules generally, but that was the general practice which was followed in preparing that list. Since the list was announced we have had, of course, a great' many representations from persons in the trade and from consumers. Those representations have been carefully considered and as a result a certain number of changes have been made. For instance, a number of things have been moved from the prohibited list into the quota list; a few have been added to the prohibited' list, but not many.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
If it is disclosed later that there is no available supply of flashlights or
flashlight batteries, I presume that under the powers which have been taken they would be moved to the other schedule?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: That is right. Power is being taken in the bill to relax these restrictions, but not to make them more onerous. The government is not asking for any power in the bill to add to the list of prohibitions, but it is asking for power to move articles from the prohibited list into the quota list or to take them out of the restricted list.

speechtext:
My hon. friend is probably as familiar as I am with the basis on which accounts are now settled between sterling area countries and Canada. The United Kingdom holds the reserves for sterling area countries. If a product is sold, let us say, to Australia, New Zealand, Egypt, India or any other country whose currency is sterling, settlement must be made for that sale unless credit terms are arranged. Over the past couple of years a substantial portion of the deficit of the sterling

Foreign Exchange Conservation
area countries has been financed out of the Canadian credit, and that credit is still operating during January, February and March.
But the deficit has always been taken care of out of either gold or convertible exchange. It is the net deficit. That was true last year and it is true now. The importing country, if it is in the sterling area, must decide how much it can afford to import from hard-currency countries. It will take into account its reserves of gold or other hard currencies, the extent to which it will be able to export goods, and so on.

Mr. MacNICbL: My friend just picked up the bag with the three oranges and threw it in the river. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
Those of course are the unfortunate incidents which I suppose cannot be helped. They can only be mitigated by customs officers exercising as much tact and courtesy as possible. The situation is that oranges are on a quota. A great many other things are prohibited. No visitor returning from the United States may bring in anything which is on the prohibited list or on the quota list. If an article is on the prohibited list no one is allowed to bring it in. If it is on the quota list the only persons allowed to import it are the holders of quotas. So unfortunately if a person goes to the United States and buys two or three heads of lettuce, as happened when I was coming up from New York a couple of weeks ago, or oranges as mentioned by my hon. friend, unless the customs officer
wants to look the other way he has to enforce the law and say, "I am sorry, but those are on the prohibited list and you will have to give them to some friend before you cross the line. You cannot bring them in." That is one of the unfortunate necessities of this unfortunate law; but it is very difficult. It would not be reasonable to give the thousands of customs officers across the country power to exercise discretion, to allow one man to bring in a prohibited article and refuse to allow another to do so. So their instructions are that if the article is on the prohibited or quota list it cannot be brought in by a person returning from the United States. That is one of the unfortunate features, but we have not been able to think of any way of avoiding it.

year, and the price compares very favourably. Of course they can also be imported from the sterling area. There is no shortage of citrus fruits this winter, and the prices are pretty good. On the question of fresh fruits and vegetables, I announced when the policy was brought in that if shortages developed, adequate supplies would be made available of the four basic vegetables, potatoes, onions, carrots and cabbages. My hon. friend is a bit older than I. I am sure if he casts his mind back he will realize that this diet of imported fresh fruits and vegetables in the winter is something of comparatively recent growth in Canada. Fifteen or twenty years ago we did not bring in fresh fruits or vegetables in the winter, from the United States or anywhere else.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: We grew our own.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: Not in the winter time. We put them down in the root cellar, but we did not grow any fresh lettuce in the winter time, or any of the other things that have been mentioned. When I was a boy I never saw a bit of fresh lettuce or any other fresh vegetable or fruit from fall until spring-the hon. member for Stanstead nods his head- and the health of the country did not suffer in those days. Our mothers used to put up all the vegetables, peas, beans, tomatoes and so on, and they were just as nutritious as these colourless things that are brought in from Mexico or somewhere else. I have had occasion to say this before but I make it now as an assertion, and I am pretty sure it is true: that the health of a single individual in Canada will not suffer because we are not bringing in S3,000,000 worth of American lettuce this winter, or some of these other pleasant, desirable but expensive things which are not essential for health purposes. When you do not have the money you have to go without some things, and that is the position we are in today quoad the United States. I will say, too, that a great many rural areas in Canada today never see a bit of fresh lettuce in the winter time, or any other fresh vegetables. They are restricted to the larger centres, where the wholesale fruit and vegetable trade can readily distribute these delicacies. But it is not general throughout Canada during the winter.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in these times of so-called austerity I am in full sympathy with the Minister of Finance, although I cannot say I am in full agreement with him. The other day one hon. member, speaking about trade, said that our trade with the United States was not as important as that with the United Kingdom and the rest of the empire. He did not make the necessary distinction. The distinction should be made between real and fictitious trade. Whether it be larger or smaller than our trade with the British commonwealth, the fact is that our trade with the United States is real trade, because the goods are sold and paid for on both sides of the border. Trade with the rest of the world is fictitious. At the present time we are living in the clouds, and the trade with the rest of the world is not at all real. Why? Precisely because of that obstacle known as the American dollar. The American dollar has become the obstacle to our trade with Americans. Surely that is incredible. The American government has been hoarding gold for a long time at Fort Knox so that it may have supremacy in trade over the whole world. It has been their avarice which has caused our difficulty and the difficulty of other countries.
The other day I made a suggestion which I believe, was quite in order; it was that we substitute barter for our present fantastic and imaginary trading processes. That would be an experience; any policy adopted for a short time is an experience. Here we are entering upon an experience in trade, and Canada has become a verboten country, as Germany was at the time of Hitler. You cannot go across the border; it is forbidden. You cannot take in any money; it is forbidden on account of our shortage of United States dollars. If
Foreign Exchange Conservation

you want a cheap refrigerator or washing machine you cannot buy it. You have to pay a tax of 25 per cent more because we have not enough reserves of United States dollars. I mention that because for a long time I have advocated sound trade policies, and I was considered unpatriotic to do that.
I find that the whole set-up of the Department of Finance is wrong. The question should not 'be to amend1 the Foreign Exchange Control Act but to get rid of it altogether. Some hon. member advocated that either yesterday or the day before when I was not in the house, but I read it in Hansard. He said that we should dispense with the Foreign Exchange Control Act. We can say a lot about imports and exports. Our import trade is an honest trade, just the same as our export trade. It affords a living to a large number of people who import goods from other countries and sell them here. But now they are precluded from doing that, precisely because we have spent too much during the war-

I am speaking only of this clause, the title of which is "import control" and the marginal note, "Goods not permitted import". My view is that we should1 dispense with this clause, dispense with the whole bill, and dispense with the foreign exchange control board.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: That is the point I raised with the hon. member. On second reading the house adapted the principle of the bill; therefore it is not in order to discuss the principle at this time. The principle has been accepted, and now we are dealing with the details of the bill, at the moment with the details of clause 3.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
I certainly do not wish to dispute with the Chair. I have too much respect for the Chair and for you personally, ' sir, to indulge in that kind of thing. But here we have clause 3, the first paragraph of which reads:
No person shall import or attempt to import into Canada any goods listed or of the classes described in schedules I II or III except in accordance with a permit issued by the minister, and, subject to this act and the regulations, the minister may issue, vary, or revoke permits for the import of such goods.

I do not object at all to the present minister exercising these powers, because I believe in his fairness and I believe he is a great Liberal. That is why I am in full sympathy with him. I realize that at times it must be pretty hard for him to defend a measure like this. But he has my entire confidence, and it is just because I want to help him that I warn him of the danger in this kind of legislation. You know very well, sir, that without speaking on the principle of the bill I can warn the committee of the danger that exists in the main clause of the bill, and if this is the main clause it is hard to make a distinction between the principle of the bill and what is contained in this clause.
What I am saying has nothing whatever to do personally with the minister or the staff of the foreign exchange control board. But I find it is bad. The best tradesman cannot expect to do a fine piece of work with a bad tool. The foreign exchange control board is a bad tool, and no one has realized yet that it is that body which keeps the whole reserve of gold and securities belonging to the Dominion of Canada. They are the ones who Jiave all the guarantees that we can give for the Canadian dollar. It is not the Bank of Canada that prints the notes; it is the foreign exchange control board that holds the fortune of the country, and that organization is not able now to meet our international financial obligations to the rest of the world. What is wrong with it? It is precisely because of the unwise management of the foreign exchange control board that that institution is unable now to render the same services that were rendered by the minister and the Department of Finance before the Bank of Canada and the foreign exchange control board were established. That is why we cannot import. There are many items in which we have no more freedom of trade. It is just as simple as spring water. This is what I object to.
How is it that if I want to buy a washing machine in the United States I have to pay from $150 to $175 for that same machine in Canada? It is because of taxation that I am compelled to pay on the supposed Canadian-made or Canadian-adjusted machine to cover our deficiency of United States dollars. It is not a complicated matter. Those who tell you this whole matter is complicated are those who will pose as experts afterwards and tell us that this subject is so very difficult that no one can understand it. Let us get down to fundamentals. Let us realize that Providence has made different climates in different countries so that the goods of those countries will be different and so that there will be an inter-

Foreign Exchange Conservation
national exchange of goods, so that there will be an inducement for men to deal together in fraternity and co-operate together. When I see obstacles made by man to prevent other men from getting what they want legitimately I am opposed to that, and I am opposed to it because I am a Liberal, and there must be a change made soon in that organization.
It is not a question of discussing the principle of the bill. It is impossible to speak on this matter without mentioning the things I have already mentioned. Of course, I am open to conviction and if something is said that will satisfy my mind I will say: Well said; I agree. But so long as such explanation is not made to me my mind is not satisfied, sir, and I say that on behalf of all the Canadians who want this country to be a free country, who want this country to be at least a country where men can trade freely with their neighbours. And mark you, sir, how is it that I cannot buy any goods from the United States because of the United States dollar when I can get the same thing from the United Kingdom, from Belgium, from France, from The Netherlands because they are not on the same currency? We pay much more for what we buy from these countries than we would pay to the United States. We have to spend more money not to use United States dollars. It does not get into my head.
I may be dumb; I may not understand the intricacies of international finance and high finance, but I do not see why I should gain nothing, why I spend twice as much to get the same thing in Canadian dollars. I cannot understand it. It is beyond me, and it is beyond the average man. Nobody understands it except the wizards in the Department of Finance, and I congratulate the minister for not being one of them. There could be no greater compliment paid to him than that. I consider him a man who means well and who wants to make a success of his department; but I am very sorry to warn him that so long as he has the same wizards around him-and I do not particularly mention the good looking gentlemen who are in front of him now; I speak of the whole organization-he will have trouble. I said that when Bennett was in power, and the same men are there today. Some newcomers have been added to the staff; but it is the same men who run the show, who are considered essential and who cannot give a satisfactory explanation to anyone.

My question is this. We have the Bank of Canada as a national institution. Is there any machinery provided by which we can convert sterling into Canadian dollars? In other words, would it not be good business to store up a surplus of sterling as a hedge
Foreign Exchange Conservation

against the day when the United States dollar slumps? We have put too much emphasis upon the United States dollar. Three-fifths of the business of the world was done in the sterling area in days gone by, and I have confidence that it will come back. Someone must be paid when he manufactures goods for export. May we not convert sterling into Canadian dollars? Are there any facilities whereby we can build up a surplus of sterling as well as United States dollars?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: We have substantial quantities of sterling now. We have made loans of something over a billion dollars. We have a loan without interest which is still outstanding. The effect of accumulating sterling, which is what my hon. friend has referred to, is simply to advance additional credit to the United Kingdom. You do not have to accumulate sterling notes in order to advance credit. It is far simpler than that. A better way to do it is by an entry in the books, and that is exactly what we have under the British credit. The net effect of exchanging Canadian dollar. bills for sterling notes, to use the example given by my hon. friend, is simply to advance that much more of a loan to the United Kingdom. The Canadian producer has to be paid in Canadian dollars. If the British importer sends over a thousand pounds to pay for something he has imported, somebody has to provide four thousand Canadian dollars to pay the Canadian exporter. If that is done by the Canadian government it is a further loan of $4,000. That is all it amounts to.

speechtext: I understand that, but the United States dollar situation does not enter into that transaction. You are going to convert it to Canadian dollars as an additional credit to the sterling area. It does not have any relationship to the United States dollar there. That is correct?

The Minister of Trade and Commerce said something about the regulations which will be brought down with respect to the motorcar industry, and he has told us about the manner in which building construction will be handled by means of projects. I am speaking for the middle class of businessmen, who ought to know now how they will be able to carry on in the time to come. I am thinking of the engineering and machine work business of the country, which went ahead 100 or 200 per cent during the war. These industries are geared to handle as great a production as they did during the war, and unless they are able to carry on with steel and iron and all the other elements that enter into their work, there will be unemployment in these industries. Last evening the minister said, referring to projects:
If the project is of any considerable size the applicant appears before the officers of the department and gives them any explanations they require.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: What is a hardship, and *who decides the question? Is it decided on the ministerial level, or by men in the departments?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
There is a departmental committee consisting of Mr. Taylor, the assistant deputy minister of finance, who is chairman, Mr. Gordon, representing the foreign exchange control board, Mr. Sim, representing customs and excise, Mr. Taggart, representing the Department of Agriculture, and Mr. Mackenzie, deputy minister of trade and commerce. All requests that come to the emergency import control division for treatment under the hardship provision are examined first by the officials of the division. They are considered by this committee, and if they fall into a pattern which has been recognized as constituting hardship they will be granted without reference to myself. If the case is unusual, and that has often been so, then the matter is referred to me with the recommendation of the committee, and I make the decision. I probably discuss the matter for some time. In one or two particular cases we had, we discussed them for nearly a week before we came to a final conclusion. Under the provision of that order in council now and under the act as drafted, I am the final judge. As I said the other night, I have
{Mr. Howe.]
to exercise something in the nature of a judicial function there. After having all the facts put before me, I have to decide whether it. is a case of exceptional hardship which merits consideration under this section.

There will be more. I have not yet had time to dictate the letters. With regard to the refrigerator problem which the hon. member for Melfort mentioned, I was going to mention that again under section 4 because I thought that was where it should be dealt with. In certain cases it does create some hardship, especial!}' in rural areas where in the last few years these cold storage plants have been put in. Encouragement has been given to the farmers to freeze their fruits, vegetables and meats; and they have to come down to get these things at the refrigerated storage. Once meats are frozen, they must be used quickly or be put in a refrigerator. People living out on a dirt road ten or fifteen miles from a cold storage plant have to bring back more than enough for one meal or for one day. These refrigerators which are operated by kerosene or gas flame are not imported in great quantity, but they are used in homes in towns w'here they are vitally necessary, more so than in the cities where there is an available ice supply or hydro supply. The hon. member said something about importing them when they were available from other countries. Of course these refrigerators can be purchased from Sweden, but they are antiquated and by the time you get them here they cost about four times as much as those being imported from the United States.
As to the possibility of making this type of refrigerator in Canada, I think it is beyond the realm of all practical possibility because it is a welded job, self-contained inside, one tube inside another, and it would be necessary to tool up to make them. The factory which makes them in the United States makes about 300,000 a year. The potential demand for refrigerators in Canada is probably about 15,000, so it would mean that the cost of your tools and dies would have to be absorbed; and it would take about fifty years to absorb the cost of your original set of tools and dies, and they would have been obsolete many years before then.

When the minister is giving consideration to hardship that has been created for certain people in rural areas, I think he should consider this at least to the extent of allowing some quota or of making some provision for gas and kerosene refrigerators for these rural territories. Of the remainder the United States supplied 213,000,000 yards. In the projected program there is provision made for only 51,000,000 yards from the United States. Needless to say, that will not fill the consumption requirements as outlined in the figures I have already mentioned.
I am making a plea for the small manufacturer who is endeavoring to produce that type of work clothes, and I would ask favourable consideration by the minister for permits to import United States denims, if applications for such permits are brought to his attention. The same argument applies to denims used in connection with sails for sailboats, awnings and other things. They are imported
to a large extent. I have particularly in mind a new manufacturer in Halifax, the Maritime Canvas Converters, who employs thirty-five men at the present time. If they do not procure the necessary yardage for the making of sails-and their export business requires sail making-the sales concerned will be cut off. This is a new business for our end of the country, and I am particularly interested in seeing that nothing be done to stop any export business or manufacturing there.
While I am on my feet, there is one other item I think I should bring to the attention of the minister in the hope that nothing will prevent a firm making rock-wool insulation from getting the material they require. The insulation is made to a large extent from seaweed, but they require a tar wrapping and1 this is procurable only in the United States. They are unable to sell their products for insulating purposes unless they have a proper covering such as a tar covering to protect the product. They have already made application which has not as yet been accepted. I trust the minister will give this application favourable consideration. So that there will be no mistake about it, the profit:ct is rock-wool insulation, made by Guilfords Limited!, of Halifax, a fine firm. I do mot know just now as to the number of men they employ. Will the minister be good' enough to take under consideration these two items, namely, United States denims and this covering for the product which I have mentioned?

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: Then I should like to know why we cannot take off the restrictions altogether as far as the United Kingdom is concerned. It would not cost us anything in United States dollars. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: I have argued this point day after day and night after night. subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: That is not my present suggestion at all. I say we could relax the restrictions, by transfers, if you like, or by amending the schedules as far as the United Kingdom is concerned. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS

You have to look into the trade statistics; you have to see what the result would be on the basis of last year's trade figures; you have to make a projection as to what it is likely to be this year, and then you make a policy decision. But that is what we have to do all the time, and I have tried to

As to hardship, that is a matter, as I said before, where in the final analysis I really have to exercise a judicial function. A hardship may be that of the importer or of the exporter or of both; or, in the third case he mentioned, a hardship suffered by some particular portion of the whole of the Canadian public. Any of these factors can be taken into consideration. But the question of hardship is qualified by the word "exceptional".
In respect of tomatoes, to which the hon. member referred, it will be understood that they were imported from Jamaica and the Bahamas. The circumstances were these, that the government of the Bahamas, through the British trade commissioner at that point, made representations to us that these tomatoes had been grown for the Canadian market, that there was no effective alternative market to which they could be sent, and that if they were not shipped to Canada a serious hardship would be caused to exporters in that country.
As my hon. friend knows, the Bahamas constitute a small community, and there are not many varieties of products available. After full consideration of all the circumstances, we came to the conclusion that import permits should be allowed for those products.	.
TMr. Abbott.]
To whom were those permits granted?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What happened was this, that the imports were arranged through Mr. Stollmeyer, the British West Indies trade commissioner. In subsection 1 (g) the governor in council is given power to make regulations suspending the operation of the act with respect to any person or any goods or any class of persons or class of goods. Without going into all the arguments which have been made since this bill first came to the house with respect to dictatorial powers and discrimination, following what was said yesterday by the minister where he stated that he disliked legislation of this type as much as anybody else did, I was wondering whether he would consider confining paragraph (g) to goods and classes of goods, leaving out reference to persons or classes of persons, thereby limiting the discrimination?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This is the purpose of that section. There must be some provision of that kind in order to enable exceptions to be made for institutions such as hospitals, or for trade fairs and matters of that kind. Admittedly it is a discretionary provision; I do not deny that. But it is very difficult to spell out any section of this kind so as to meet all the cases which one may wish to meet.
It will be noted that this is a relaxing provision. If authorized by the regulations, the minister may relax these restrictions. It is true that it would open the door to favouritism, if the minister were so inclined. But I really believe that, on balance, it is better to leave it in these general terms, thereby allowing reasonable freedom to the administration to relax these restrictions in cases such as I have mentioned, or in such other cases as it may be deemed proper to take such action. If the power were exercised unwisely, I should hope we would hear about it in the house.
I should have added that this can be exercised only in virtue of a regulation published

in the Canada Gazette and tabled in the House of Commons, so that the public will be enabled to see in what circumstances these relaxing powers are exercised.

I appreciate that, also the spirit of the ministers remarks, but I ask again whether he does not think the retention of the words "any goods or class of goods," gives him the discretionary power which he envisages.

That is the way in which the regulation would have to be drafted. I do not think there could be a general regulation exempting anybody that the minister might determine. This is purely an enabling power giving the governor in council power to exempt by regulation any person or any goods or any class of goods. speechtext: As my hon. friend will appreciate, the great majority of the people in Canada are not importers. Another matter is not quite clear to me. The minister said that the trade will be allocated according to certain percentages. Take textiles, for instance-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The 400 per cent is a global quota. In the base period, textiles were imported to the amount of $10,301,000 from schedule countries, from dollar countries. Four hundred per cent of that is roughly $40,000,000. Imports in the base period were $128,525,000. Forty million divided into the figure I just gave gives us approximately 32 per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

imports of textiles in the base period 1937-39: scheduled countries, $10,301,000; non-scheduled countries, $30,591,000; total $40,892,000. These were the total imports from scheduled and non-scheduled countries in the base period of 1937-39. That is the average for these years.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The total is $40,892,000. That was the global quota. The global quota is 400 per cent of the average imports in the period 1937-39, and taking the scheduled countries, which are the ones we are interested in, the dollar countries, 400 per cent of $10,301,000 is approximately $40,000,000, something in excess of $40,000,000. Subsection 3 of section 5 is a peculiar one. Perhaps the minister can explain it. It reads as follows:
Where the governor in council is of opinion that any goods not included in schedules I, II or III, are being imported into Canada for use or consumption in substitution for any goods included in those schedules, respectively, the governor in council may by regulation prescribe that such goods shall be deemed to be included in schedule I, II or III, as the ease may be, in which the goods for which the said goods are so substituted, are included.
What is the import of the subsection? Is it a case of there being some subterfuge in the importer bringing in goods which will defeat the purposes of the act, or what?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Broadly speaking, that is about right, yes. That is pretty much a standard provision in all customs acts at the present time. If you prohibit the import of an article you have a provision in your act to the effect that if something is manufactured which is in effect a substitute for that, although it may not come within the technical definition of the tariff item, it, is then treated in exactly the same way. In other words, substitute goods stand on the same footing, prohibition or quota, as the case may be, as the goods which are set out specifically in the tariff item.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Perhaps that can be considered when we come to section 9. I have given some thought to the suggestion made by the hon. member for Rosedale and, in so far as it is possible to do it, I am sure it would be desirable that it should be done, but I question whether it is really practicable. I do not quite see how it would work out except for broad categories such as the automobile industry or the electrical industry. Where an application is made to import a printing press, I find it hard to see how one could lay down a general principle, except the principle of the appreciation of all the circumstances, first, as to whether it is necessary in Canada, and, second, as to whether it would contribute either to greater export trade or to production in Canada which would save imports.
It merely protects the liberty of the individual, which is the paramount consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend is speaking in generalities. I am as much interested in the liberty of the individual as anyone else in this house; but I am trying to look at the matter from a practical point of view to see what we can do, and speaking from legal experience I do not see how one could set up case law in the administration of a schedule such as schedule III. If it were possible I would be glad to do it.

May I ask a question about a suggestion I made to the minister, which has been described as trading cattle for cabbages? The minister knows what I refer to; but to refresh his memory, I may say it occurred to me that he would be the gainer under the act if he were to allow a certain number of cattle to be exported to the United States and, with the proceeds received from those cattle, he could purchase $8,000,009 worth of cabbages, lettuce, beets, carrots, and one or two other vegetables which I enumerated on a former occasion. There would probably be a net United States income in the result, and among the premises on which I based the suggestion was the fact that when people are as much accustomed as the people of Canada are to a certain diet and cannot get salads, they choose some substitute other than more potatoes or additional bread. They eat more meat or fish and such fruit as can be imported. So that if the meat that would otherwise be consumed and would not be available for export to Britain, and the fish as well, were sent to the United States, where there is a hungry market for these commodities, we would have funds with which to, supply the normal and nutritious diet which the Canadian people expect and rightfully expect. The minister knows of the suggestion,, and I should like to know what the departmental officials have said regarding it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have listened with attention to my hon. friend's remarks and I am afraid I have no special comment to offer on them.

I should like to have an answer to the suggestion. It is a constructive one and, as far as one can see without having all the details of administration presented to one, there is no reason why it should not be considered. I do not make this suggestion for the simple purpose of speaking, and I wish to have an answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Like all my hon. friend's suggestions, it will be considered.

The minister does not realize the nature of these regulations. If he had some idea of what constitutes the normal

Tribute to Mr. Kenneth Cragg

healthy diet of the Canadian people-not the diet he said he was brought up on, so healthy and apparently so adequately, but the normal diet recommended by his own colleague the Minister of National Health and leading nutritionists-he would realize that among the articles specified are fresh leafy green vegetables daily. That is recommended by nutritionists throughout the world. .The minister endeavours to make out a case on. the theory' that, because our forefathers did not have certain things, we do not need them. I might remind him that the turnip was discovered1 by Lord Townshen-d for the express purpose of feeding cattle over the winter. Otherwise, cattle had to be slaughtered, but he developed turnips for this purpose, and that is why we can keep stock in cold climates from one season to another. The world progresses. I do not wish to take up time unduly, but if the minister does not give me an answer I shall be compelled to enumerate some of the principles of nutrition as outlined by Parran, surgeon general of the United States, and other nutritionists throughout the world. If 'the minister undertakes to get an answer from his officials in regard' to the suggestion I made, of trading cattle for cabbages, I shall be glad to -resume my seat and keep it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am afraid we shall have to listen to my hon. friend's views on nutrition.. I cannot give and do not intend to give a further answer.
Section, agreed to.
On section 6-Ministerial power to prescribe procedure, forms, etc.

Mr. Chairman, before this clause is taken up by the committee, might I be given an opportunity to say something by way of privilege at this time, concerning a -matter which, I am sure, is very' close -bo your heart, as it is to mine. It could not be brought up in the formal session of the house, having regard- to the established amenities of parliament, but I now crave the indulgence of this committee for a moment or so.
The press gallery of this parliament is an integral part of our parliamentary institutions and our parliamentary machinery. Its members are very close to us in our work, in. our friendships and in our affections. There have been few 'instances since I came to the house, or since you -came into it, Mr. Chairman, in which we have lost one of the members of the press gallery while the house was actually in session, and 'because of the cloud which has been cast- over -the -parliamentary scene

by the death yesterday of an outstanding correspondent, -the late Mr. Kenneth Cragg, I should like to pay a tribute to his memory, if I ma.v do so on this occasion..
He was a very close friend of yours, Mr. Chairman, as he was of mine and of many other members on all sides of the house. Mr. Cragg was an outstanding journalist. He was a widely-read author; a kindly and witty philosopher; a fine public-spirited Canadian; a devoted husband and father. The sudden passing yesterday of this illustrious Canadian removed a man while he was y-et in harness; and perhaps he died in the way in which he would have wished'.
He was parliamentary correspondent for the Globe and Mail for five years and, while in that position, as -in previous positions which he filled so well, he had built up a high reputation for newsy, accurate, fair and broadminded writing and reporting from here and elsewhere. Throughout his journalistic career his agricultural background kept peeping out from behind in almost every story he wrote for public consumption. I think that added to the richness and the value of the contributions he so liberally made to the public in general. Written under the handicap of most indifferent health, his most recent volume called "Father on the Farm" has cheered the lives and revived the memories of many thousands of Canadians whose interest in agriculture has never flagged nor failed, regardless of the avocation to which they later went during their lifetime. That work is in a class of its owTn and its author has made a contribution of a signal character to the Canadian literature of our time.
The press gallery will miss one of its most popular personalities; the Globe and Mail, one of its high-class journalists; parliament, one of its most honest and interesting commentators, and Canada, one of her finest native sons. Hon. members on all sides of the house this afternoon will, I am sure, want to pause to pay tribute to the life and work of Kenneth Cragg and- to extend to Mrs. Cragg, Brian and Katherine, his father and his aunt, our deep and genuine sympathy in this their sad hour of trouble and sorrow.

In view of the close association which Mr. Cragg has always maintained with agriculture I wish to speak, on behalf of the government and I am sure I speak on behalf of all members on this side of the house, in agreement with all that has been said by the hon. member for Peel. Since coming to the House of Commons, I have never been more shocked than I was yester-

Tribute to Mr. Kenneth Cragg
day when it was announced to my office that Mr. Cragg had passed on. He was in my office just shortly before, as he has been often ever since he has been associated with the gallery during my time in Ottawa. Scarcely a week has gone by that he has not been in to inquire with regard to agricultural matters. I wish to say that all the reports he has made on matters having to do with agriculture, and more particularly with regard to anything that has been said in this house, from any side of it, on behalf of agriculture, have been made in a manner which not only did credit to the paper for which he wrote but showed a consideration for and understanding of farmers throughout Canada-and throughout the world for that matter-which is shown by very few who write on public matters.
On one occasion I had the privilege of driving with him over a considerable part of the province of Manitoba; and at other times over other sections of Canada. I always found him most anxious to become correctly informed as to the life of people on the farm. Anyone who has read his delightful book cannot avoid being impressed with the knowledge which he himself had through experience with persons who are typical farmers. Anyone who has had the home experience that he must have had in order to make it possible to write a book of the kind, is in a position to speak for and of farmers in a manner which few others can. I think not only this house but Canada, and more particularly that section of Canada for which he wrote daily, has suffered a great loss in the passing of this revered late member of the press gallery. I join with everything that has been said by the hon. member for Peel in paying our respects and tribute to him and in passing on our sympathy to his immediate family.

Might I be allowed, Mr. Chairman, on behalf of this group to join in the expressions of sympathy to the family and relatives of the late Mr. Cragg. Mr. Cragg was one of the few members of the press gallery whom I could call my personal friend. It was always a pleasure to meet him and to talk with him. Such was his nature that I think he would be indeed surprised to hear the comments that have been made today in this house in regard to his character. I am glad to be able to associate the members of this group with what was so well said by both the Minister of Agriculture and the hon. member for Peel.

I feel that I should associate the group I represent with all that has been said so well by other speakers in connection
with the untimely passing of this member of the press gallery. Being one of the newer members of the House of Commons I did not have the privilege of knowing Mr. Cragg very well. But I feel sure that I am expressing the sentiments of all my group in associating ourselves with what has been said and in expressing our sincere sympathy to those who are left to mourn him.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The committee will now revert to the consideration of the bill. We are considering section 6.

Section 6, subsection 1, paragraph (c) reads as follows:
(c) in particular cases or classes of cases, from time to time, prescribe terms of, and conditions to a permit or the permission granted in a permit additional to those prescribed by regulation.
Will the minister, if he will, explain the-necessity for taking power to vary the terms or conditions of a permit in addition to those which are prescribed by the regulation? Surely he will be able to do all he wants to do under the regulation, without taking this additional authority.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The difficulty there is this. As my hon. friend points out, the section is fairly broad in its terms. Here is a case where it is felt that it may be necessary' to issue a ministerial direction. A quota holder has a certain quota for oranges or whatever you like. He proceeds to sell those in an area close to home, where perhaps it is a little more profitable, and he does not continue to supply the customers he has been in the habit of supplying. It is similar to the provision we made for equitable distribution during the war, where the Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation, in importing goods, took steps to see that there was equitable distribution through the normal trade channels. Then again a man may have a quota-I am just citing examples-on textiles, which is a dollar quota. Instead of importing staples such as denim for overalls, and so on, he may go into high-grade textiles for bedspreads, or something like that. I am advised it is almost essential that there should be some power to impose, as a condition of the continuance of the quota, that it should be exercised equitably in relation to the import of goods by other people. It might be possible to phrase that section in a better way; I do not know. I have been worrying about it myself, but I have outlined to the committee why that power is needed. I freely concede it is one which can be abused; there is no doubt about that, but I am afraid that is also true of some other provisions.

Foreign Exchange Conservation

I think this is a startling departure. It shows how easy it is to follow the downward path. There was a period when we were, scandalized, I was going to say, by government by order in council. That seemed a radical departure from the rule of law as we understood it. This section empowers the minister who is in charge of its operation to follow his own whim. He does not even require an order in council; he does not even require a regulation. In fact there may be a regulation or an order in council to the contrary, but in the exercise of the discretion which is his he may determine what transaction may be entered into. But it does not stop there. If the minister is otherwise occupied anyone else who is in his service may exercise these extraordinary powers for him.
I submit that it is time to call a halt. Whatever may be the emergency-and I am not going to worry my hon. friends opposite with the ease with which they produce emergencies -arising out of this situation, it is an unimportant matter compared with the urgencies of war. Yet when the country's very existence was in the balance the government did not ask for the latitude which is exacted and taken in this section.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: We had far more latitude during the war. We did not even require an act.

The minister is quite a latitudinarian, I admit, and we could probably find instances in which his interpretation of the law has been generous as far as his own powers were concerned. But I would be very much amazed if the minister could point to any statute in which a similar provision appears. This paragraph (c) of subsection 1 gives the minister power to act against the law and in spite of the law; I suggest to the government, with such seriousness as I can command, that it abandon this final encroachment upon the liberty of the citizen. The citizen must know the law; he is supposed to know the law; it is his duty to know the law. What opportunity is there for him to know the law? Somebody has said the law is fickle, but here the law is nothing but the whim of the departmental employee who exercises discretion under the minister. I submit that this means there is no possibility of knowing the law or of complying with the law. It is the negation of the rule of law.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not suppose this will command this provision to my hon. friend, but there is a similar section in identical terms in the Foreign Exchange Control Act.
Would the minister be good enough to point it out? I am always looking for light.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes. It is section 36 (1):
Subject to the provisions of this act and the regulations and under the control and direction of the minister, the board may
(b)	in particular cases or classes of cases, from time to time prescribe terms and conditions for permits additional to those prescribed by regulation or prescribe special forms of permits in cases where none is prescribed by regulation.
Surely the minister is not going to argue that the passage he has just read is comparable with paragraph (c) in this bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Almost word for word. That is where it was taken from.
I would point out to the hon. gentleman'-and he is far from lacking in powers of observation-that the board is, to begin with, something quite different from the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The board is the creature of the minister, the agent of the minister.

We have had reason to complain of that, too; but the board is supposed to be a composite entity which meets and keeps minutes of its deliberations and has to put them on record. This paragraph reads:
Subject to this act and the regulations, the minister may
(c)	in particular cases or classes of cases, from time to time, prescribe terms of, and conditions to a permit or the permission granted in a permit additional to those prescribed by regulation.
If that means anything it means the minister can tear up the regulations whenever it pleases him. I submit, with great deference and respect to the hon. gentleman who is conducting this bill through the house, that the provision which is found ini the Foreign Exchange Control Act, and which has gotten us into enough trouble, is altogether different, altogether more restricted than the clause before us at the moment.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: In the drafting of this bill, or since, has consideration been given to altering this section so as to make it read that these regulations would be made by the governor in council?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Perhaps I should explain that the regulations are made and must be approved by the governor in council. This section covers acts which the minister may do, apart from regulations. The first of these is to prescribe the procedure to be followed in applying for and issuing permits. That is pretty much an administrative job, namely, filling out form number so and so. Then, it is to ,prescribe forms necessary for the administration of the act.
Before the dinner recess we were discussing paragraph (c) which contains, I concede, very broad powers to be exercised by the minister in dealing with individual cases. It is a power similar to that contained in the Foreign Exchange Control Act, the board in that instance being the agent of the minister.
I have given, personally, a great deal of thought to this paragraph, wondering how it might be framed in terms which would lay down some definite criteria as to the basis upon which the minister may act. But this is an extraordinarily difficult thing to do.
As I have said, the purpose is to enable fair treatment to be exercised between different importers. Perhaps by way of illustration I might read to the committee an alternative section which I had drafted, and which might commend itself as being less objectionable in form than the one which now appears in the bill. It would read in this way:
(c) In particular eases or classes of cases, where it is advisable in order to ensure that
(i)	the import of goods by a person pursuant to a permit is carried on equitably in relation to the import of goods by other persons to whom permits have been granted,
or,
(ii)	goods imported pursuant to permits are distributed so as to be available equitably to consumers
prescribe, from time to time, terms of and conditions to a permit or the permission granted in a permit additional to those prescribed by regulation;
That would set out the cases in which the minister might exercise that discretion in conformity, of course, with the provisions of the act and of the regulations which have to be approved by order in council. As I say, after discussing the matter thoroughly with those who were charged with the administration of similar provisions under wartime measures, and who will be charged with
administration in this instance, it was felt that it is almost essential for the efficient administration of the act that discretion should be vested in someone to deal with individual cases.
In the case of the foreign exchange control board it is vested in the board which, after all, is merely the agent of the minister. It did seem to me that it was better here to place the responsibility squarely upon the minister. It is true that in practice it would be exercised by some one whom he would delegate to do it. In the particular circumstances we have here, the head of the emergency import control division is one of the assistant deputy ministers, Mr. Taylor. That is the explanation of this paragraph (c).
I believe it is fair to say that it is the only subsection here which, in form, is objectionable as perhaps conveying somewhat too broad powers.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
The minister has said two things which, it seems to me, strengthen our argument that this power should not stay solely in the hands of the minister. He has indicated that it will be difficult to indicate the criteria to be laid down; and he has also admitted that paragraph (c) as it now stands gives the minister very broad powers indeed. For these reasons it seems to me that the minister himself should want the protection of at least having to take this matter to his colleagues in the cabinet.
Things have moved a great deal in this parliament. It is not long since we were blasting against the idea of government by order in council. But here we have reached the point where so much power is being placed in the hands of a minister that we would welcome a return to the earlier days when ministers had at least to get the definite and specific approval of their colleagues in the cabinet in the form of orders in council.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I would gladly do that. I raised exactly the same question my hon. friend has raised when I was discussing the matter with my advisers. I said, "Surely these cases would not be so numerous that I could not make individual submissions to council each time in respect of hardship cases or cases of inequitable distribution". They assured me that in practice it was found, when similar questions arose in connection with wartime prices and trade board regulations, that, of necessity, there must be discretion in someone to act promptly in these individual cases.
It is not desired to have this power in order to be arbitrary in the administration of the

Foreign Exchange Conservation
act. It is to enable hardship cases to be dealt with promptly and to make sure that, if a man has a quota and he is not living up to his obligations under it, he can be forced to do so.
As I say, in view of my own philosophy in these matters, I am just about as much worried-or probably I should say bothered- by the broad general powers as is any member in the committee. But I cannot avoid being influenced by the advice I am given by people in whose judgment in these matters I have implicit confidence, because I have seen the responsibilities they have to carry.
If the committee felt that this should be a matter to be dealt with by regulation, which would mean individual submissions to council, I do not know that I could resist too strongly. I think I should be bound to say, however, that I believe it is more desirable to do it the other way.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I am glad to know the minister is bothered about it the way it stands. My further submission is that underlying this whole business of placing so much power in the hands of the minister is the notion that this is an exceedingly temporary piece of legislation. I am afraid that the disequilibrium of world trade is something that may be with us for some considerable time, or until we take more effective measures than these to deal with it, and that it is unwise to go ahead on that premise.
There is always the danger-and it does work out that way-that powers which we give to individuals temporarily, stay there for a very long time. I hope the minister will give the matter further thought.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will. This very paragraph is primarily directed against quota permits, or the administration of the quota permits system, which has some complexities in its day-to-day administration. As I say, I have a suggested alternative to paragraph (c) which I think lays down pretty definitely the criteria which must govern in the exercise of these discretionary powers. But I do urge strongly that the committee leave that discretion in there because, as I repeat, I am assured by those who have the onerous task of administration that it is an essential thing to the smooth and effective administration of the act, in the interests, not of the people who have the administration of it, but rather in the interests of those who are subject to its administration.

I appreciate what the minister has said respecting the administration of the act. I also appreciate what was said by the hon. member for Stanstead and the
TMr. Abbott.]
hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. It seems to me that paragraph (c) of subsection 1 of section 61 is particularly objectionable because of paragraph (d), whereby the minister can delegate these extraordinary powers to some person who is not responsible to parliament. Might I suggest to the minister that he delete paragraph (c) altogether, or, if not, that he add by way of amendment the following words: "except as to the powers of the minister granted in this section".

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would not object to accepting that last suggestion. I think it is desirable under the administration section to give the minister power to delegate his authority but not power to exercise discretionary powers conferred by section 6.
That was my suggestion. Would the minister move an amendment accordingly?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Perhaps in order to cover it I might ask one of my colleagues to move the more restrictive language which I indicated to the committee by way of amending paragraph (c) and a consequential amendment to paragraph (d) to exclude from its operation the discretion exercised under paragraph (c).
Just what would paragraph (d) cover?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The actual granting of the permit and other routine details in connection with administration. Perhaps that is necessarily implied; I do not know. I am told that it is usual to have this provision in the administration section. There is a great deal of routine work such as the signing of permits. There are some 7,000 quotas, I am informed. It is that sort of thing. I would hate to have to put my signature to all these quotas.

Would not the power to sign permits be covered by section 6 (1) (a), which gives the minister power to prescribe the procedure to be followed in applying for and issuing permits? On the other hand, this very wide power given in paragraph (d) authorizes any person under the minister's control and direction to act for him. That is a wide-open power to delegate, and I suggest that it is not necessary.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is qualified by the words, "under his control and direction". The minister must always take the responsibility. He must accept responsibility for the acts of those whom he appoints to act for him. Section 3 (1) provides that the minister may issue, vary, or revoke permits, and so on and

Foreign Exchange Conservation
-so forth. I do not think that is a dangerous provision. Frankly, it did not give me special concern. But, again frankly, section 6 (1) (c) did. I felt that it was including broad discretionary powers which were pretty sweeping.

I suggest, in support of the hon. member for Kindersley, that the minister make his amendment to 6 (1) (c) and delete 6 (1) (d) altogether. I do not think any harm will be done to the efficient administration of the act by deleting paragraph (d).

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am told that a similar power is contained in a great many acts, and not only war emergency acts. The treasury solicitor tells me that. I cannot speak from personal knowledge, but I would hesitate to strike out the paragraph without consulting the legal advisers to see what the possible effect might be. Perhaps in the meantime my colleague would move the amendment to paragraph (c).
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I move:
That paragraph (c) of section 6(1) be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"(c) in particular cases or classes of cases, where it is advisable in order to ensure that
(i)	the import of goods by a person pursuant to a permit is carried on equitably in relation to the import of goods by other persons to whom permits have been granted, or
(ii)	goods imported pursuant to permits are distributed so as to be available equitably to consumers
prescribe, from time to time, terms of and conditions to a permit or the permission granted in a permit additional to those prescribed by regulation."

The amendment is long and somewhat involved; if the minister has not copies available I suggest that it stand until copies can be printed and circulated, and we can come back to the clause later this evening.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: It is proposed that 6(1) (c) stand for the time being.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
And there was a consequential amendment to 6(1) (d), Mr. Chairman. I would ask my colleague to move it.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I move:
That 6(1) (d) be amended by adding thereto the following:
"except in the exercise of the powers conferred by this section."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That can stand until tomorrow.
Can the minister give any further instances in which this power under paragraph (d) would be required?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: If we attempt to decentralize, which we must in the administration of capital goods schedules, and permits were to be issued, say in Vancouver, it would be necessary to delegate to someone in Vancouver the powers of the minister to issue permits. My hon. friend smiles, but there will be about 15,000 permits a month required. They could not all be issued from a central office. The department has branch offices today which are being equipped to issue permits.
The power the minister requires is given under 6(1)(a), by which he may prescribe the procedure to be followed in applying for and issuing permits.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: A legal question is involved. I do not think it would override the specific provision of clause 3, "except in accordance with a permit issued by the minister." It is open to question; I do not know.

I take it that the minister has in mind appointing someone to act under himself as a sort of head of a permit issuing body. May I suggest that any such official should be restricted in his powers of making what are virtually orders in council such as was done under the wartime prices and trade board. Their orders were issued over the signature of Donald Gordon. I have no doubt he had the orders drawn and submitted them to the minister, who gave them his blessing on the say-so of Donald Gordon and then gave them the force of law by order in council. We have often pointed out on this side of the house that in too many cases the ordinary rights of the individual to defend himself in court were taken away by those orders.
I urge that the minister in administering this part of the act should make certain that when orders in council are drawn creating regulations these regulations should be gone over by his law officers or by the law officers of the crown, and carefully considered, and that they should1 not be the brain child of a single individual who may be as smart as any child of Adam could possibly be. I suggest that the regulations which are made by orders in council* should be carefully considered, possibly not by t'he minister who will not have time to do that, but at least by more than one law officer of the crown. In the past, under the wartime prices and trade board regulations the orders in council were, in my opinion at least, the brain child of some [DOT]expert who did not know all that he thought he knew.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
May I say to my hon. friend, from experience extending over five or six years during the war, with fairly close

Foreign Exchange Conservation
contact certainly with the wartime prices and trade board regulations, all these regulations were pretty carefully considered) not only by the law officers of the crown but by the minister, and in many cases by his parliamentary assistant, and that they were not in any case the brain child of any one individual. Here there is no power on the part of anyone to make regulations. The regulations have to be adopted by the governor in council. The wartime prices and trade board particularly had power as a board to make certain orders. That, of course, is not the case here.
May I revert for a moment to the point raised by the hon. member for Vancouver South. I am advised by the treasury solicitor, who is in front of me, that the only power which the minister would have to delegate under section 6, paragraph (d)1, with the amendment as proposed, relates to the issue of the permits. There is no other power in the act which he is given and which he would have the power to delegate.
Would the minister be willing to put in paragraph (d) that the power is only to apply to the issuing of permits?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It relates only to permits; it might relate to the detail in connection with the issuing of permits. It might cover a little wider territory than the actual signing of the permits. I have already proposed an amendment which excludes from its operation the exercise of this discretion conferred under paragraph (c). That must be exercised by the minister personally if the amendment which I propose carries; therefore I am informed that the remaining discretionary power in the minister as minister is in connection with the issue of permits that he can delegate, subject to his control and direction. But that is the only power given to the minister as a minister as distinct from what is to be done by order in council. Therefore, subject to check, I think my hon. friend's point is met.
If a person or firm makes an application for a permit and is turned down, is there any appeal from that decision?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, there is in this sense. If he is turned down in the ordinary routine course by the officials of the emergency import control division, then there is an appeal to the minister, and I have had a good many cases of that kind.
Under what section?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It does not have to be under any section, because I am the only one who has the power to issue permits. It is the

minister who does it. If the applicant is not satisfied with the action of the minister's subordinates he is entitled in every case to go to the top.
If an applicant felt that he had something further on his case he could go to the minister?
