But I wish to consider the question from a broad point of view. Is it physically possible for any minister to decide personally all the questions that may arise regarding matters that are within the sphere of his department? It is a physical impossibility. Then, naturally, the matter will be decided by some minor officials in the name of the minister and the minister will be just a rubber-stamp for decisions made by some major or minor officer in his department. This is the situation as it stands, and as one who is a strong supporter of responsible government I cannot accept that kind of legislation.
Perhaps I shall be called regressive. They will say that I am not a modern, that I am obsolete when I say there are certain ancient things that we should keep in mind, things that are ageless. They do not belong to some other age because they belong to all ages. For example, there are certain fundamentals of law which were promulgated three thousand years ago and which are still accepted by the legal fraternity and by the bench in these modern times, and1 one of these principles is that of responsible government. The minister is for it, and I would be greatly surprised if the Minister of Trade and Commerce were not for it also. We are all for it. Then let us practise it.
There is a good way of being in order, Mr. Chairman, in discussing any part of this bill; namely, to move that some clause be struck out; the matter will be decided and anyone will have an opportunity to say anything he has to say. I forecast some time ago certain things that would happen, and today they have come to pass. But I was not the only one. There was a member of the press gallery, the president of the press gallery last year,

who wrote splendid articles in his paper, and I said what I had to say in the House of Commons. Now it has come true.
In these times of so-called austerity how is it that we can buy chocolates which are imported from Europe and which sell at $2 a pound? How is it that in these times of austerity we are offered certain biscuits at $1 a half-pound? These are times of austerity and there are other commodities that are needed. For instance, if we go to a store to buy a head of lettuce having five or six leaves, we pay thirty or thirty-five cents for it, or about five cents a leaf. They are good to look at but not to buy. Nothing has been said about that.
We cannot take all the individual facts with regard to all possible imports, I know; but I cannot understand how it is that certain imports are so expensive, for one reason or another. For example, a bottle of French brandy bought for SI.50 in France is sold in Canada at S6.50. It is very expensive, because we cannot buy brandy from the United States. And so on.
I am ready to accept any explanation which I can convey to my constituents to satisfy their minds about this legislation, because at present they are angry. I am sure the minister is not responsible for the drafting; but he is responsible for the bill, and I make that necessary distinction. I give him credit for anything for which I can give him credit. I sympathize with him. I regret that he has to sponsor this legislation. I will tell you more than that, Mr. Chainnan. I do not consider that I, as a Liberal party man, am bound by this legislation any more than I was bound by the foreign exchange control legislation, because I was never consulted about it. I consider that I am bound by the policies of the party to the extent that I, as a member, am consulted with the other members of the party and the decision is reaohed according to that of the majority of the party. (d) prescribing conditions to the issue of permits, and terms of, and conditions to permits or the permissions granted by permits, and terms of and conditions to the continuation of permits in effect.

(c.) in particular cases or classes of cases, where it is advisable in order to ensure that
(i)	the import of goods by a person pursuant to a permit is carried on equitably in relation to the import of goods by other persons to whom permits have been granted, or

prescribe, from time to time, terms of and conditions to a permit or the permission granted in a permit additional to those prescribed by regulation.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, I think it was, earlier this evening pointed out the fact that we had been complaining of order by governor in council. Now we have piled on top of order by governor in council, power to give the minister the right to amend the orders in council as he sees fit. It seems to me that this is going too far altogether. As the hon. member for Stanstead said some time ago, the whole procedure is unconstitutional, and it seems to me that it should not be permitted for one instant. It should not be permitted in this or any other act. Under the proposed amendment, the words are, "in particular cases or classes of cases," but there is no definition in the act saying what

those words mean. I should like the minister to define those words for us and let us know just what he means by them. Further on, these words are used: "is carried on equitably;" that the import of goods by a person pursuant to a permit is "carried on equitably." WThat does he mean by those words? There is no definition in the bill, and I think we should have more light thrown on it. This afternoon and this evening I have been glancing through the report of a committee on ministers' powers, I think known as the Sankey report, made in 1932 by a committee of the British House of Commons. In the course of that report, which it quite voluminous and interesting, I find this:
The truth is that if parliament were not willing to delegate lawmaking power, parliament would be unable to pass the kind and quantity of legislation -which modern public opinion requires.
But it goes on to point out:
We doubt, however, whether parliament itself has fully realized how extensive the practice of delegation has become, or the extent to which it has surrendered its own functions in the process, or how easily the practice might be abused.
There are contained in the report certain recommendations, of which this is No. 2, at page 65:
The precise limits of the lawmaking power which parliament intends to confer on a minister should always be expressly defined in clear language by the statute which confers it, when discretion is conferred; its limits should be defined with equal clearness.
I submit that the section, with the amendment now proposed, does not define with any clearness the limits of the discretion it is proposed to confer on the minister. The terms could not be broader. There is no limitation whatever. Altogether apart from that, however, I submit that this legislation is vicious and unconstitutional, and I am not prepared to vote for it.

speechtext: He can dispose of his permit and the quota will go with it if the purchaser buys the business as a going concern. The purpose of the section is to prevent trafficking in quotas, as distinct from the business itself.

When I learned about this a couple of weeks ago I was informed by a friend that there was a certain amount of

On section 10-Offences and penalties.

I wish to state an objection to section 10 as briefly as I can. It looks to me as if it is another one of those sections under which, in prosecutions, accused persons will not have a very good1 chance of succeeding. What I object to in respect of these prosecutions-and it is becoming altogether too prevalent not only in connection with federal statutes but also in connection with provincial statutes-is that the old British practice of proving mens rea, or guilty mind, or guilty knowledge, is too often being ignored. I maintain that it is being ignored1 purely and simply because of laziness. I think it is laziness on the part of crown officials or police. Surely to goodness, it is not any more difficult to prove a man guilty of an offence of 'this type than it is to prove him guilty of any other criminal offence.
For years and centuries it has been the right of every man to be presumed' innocent until he is proven guilty. And he can be convicted only if he is proven guilty of an offence with a guilty mind, with the intention of doing wrong. Beyond any question of doubt, cases which have gone to the courts of appeal now hold that a mere innocent infraction of a section such as this makes a man, a citizen of this country, liable to the heavy penalty provided by the section.

So far as I am concerned, I would1 never vote for a section like this until the minister agreed to put in a safeguard incorporating the old principle of mens rea, stating that that principle must be proven; that the burden of proof must be assumed1 by crown officers, and that a man who innocently disobeys one of these regulations-and there were thousands of them under the wartime prices and trade board-must have mens rea proven against him. Under the wartime prices and trade board I believe there were about 35,000 orders in council under which people could be prosecuted. It was absolutely ridiculous to imagine that a private citizen of this country; yes, it was ridiculous to imagine that even lawyers could have any possible conception or knowledge of a half, a third', a tenth, a twentieth or even a hundredth of those regulations. And the poor man could be brought up in court-and I 'have defended lots of them-and the court might know that man was innocent, and I would know he was innocent, so far as his mind and heart were concerned. But they were convicted, and were virtually made criminals with criminal records, although, in their hearts and minds, they had no intention of wrongdoing against the laws of this country.
I think we must take a stand; and I plead with members of this committee, and especially the legal members, to give some thought to this matter. It is getting too serious. Citizens of this country should not have to run the risk of innocently disobeying laws of which they may have no knowledge whatsoever. The promulgation of them is such that it could not be possible for them to have any such knowledge. Those people, in my humble judgment, should not be convicted of offences against the laws of this country and be tagged virtually with criminal records.
I strongly object to section 10 in this bill unless the burden of proof of guilt is clearly, by the section, placed upon the crown officers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I bow to my hon. friend's superior knowledge of criminal law, with which I cannot claim to be expert. However. I feel it might meet his objection if the word "knowingly" were inserted, so that it would read, "every person who knowingly" does so and so.
Consciously.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think the word "knowingly" would be preferable.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I anticipated an objection similar to this one. Analogous provisions are found throughout the criminal code in connection with the excise regulations, narcotics, and other matters, and a good many of them are statutes which have been on the statute books for a long time. Broadly speaking, the fundamental rule is that the burden of proof rests upon the person who is asserting guilt in a criminal case. There are two exceptions which are recognized in English criminal law. The first is where it requires a person to prove a negative, which is frequently exceedingly difficult, although proof of positive facts may not be so difficult. The second case is where facts are peculiarly within the knowledge of the other party.
Anyone here would know whether he had a permit or not. In these acts which require a permit, and this applies to a greater number of provisions in the Excise Act, the Narcotic Drugs Act, and in the criminal code, the onus is on the person charged with the offence to show that he does possess a permit. That has been particularly necessary in cases where, as here, permits are issued from one side of the country to the other by customs collectors acting as agents for the foreign exchange control board, or by some other government agency. I am quite willing to add the word "knowingly" to meet my hon. friend's point, so that the onus would be on the crown in the case of an innocent person who inadvertently contravenes the law. I do not think anybody can quarrel very much with that. I think that should go a long way toward overcoming the objection.
Yes, so far as I am concerned.

The enactments which are found in the Customs Act and in the Excise Act and in most of the acts in which the crown is the victim of illegal practices are drawn in such a way that the burden of proof is shifted to the accused. I suggest to the minister that legislation of that type, which is age-old, and with which people have had years to become acquainted, is hardly on a parity with these rules and regulations and orders in council which can come into existence without notice and frequently, as hon. members will recall, without even the knowledge of the minister. I do not wish to be facetious or to trifle with the difficulties of administration which confront the treasury benches at this time; but everybody must

admit that legislation such as is being passed tonight is an invitation to irregularity, an invitation to the smuggler, an invitation to those who will profit improperly by this enactment. We are not seeking to protect a body of malefactors; but there is something that should be protected, and that is the innocence of a person who may be improperly charged with breaking the law.
The law is going to be the regulations, modified as indicated by the minister. It is absolutely impossible for the people at large, and I was going to say for the ministry itself, to keep abreast of all these regulations and their modifications. Modifications will take place in one part of the country which will not be known in the other part for some time. We are exposing the population of Canada to a loss of confidence in the courts and in the judiciary if we place upon any person who is apprehended the burden of showing he is not guilty. It seems to me that, in the Customs and Excise Acts, it would be better for everyone if the rules were abandoned and if we relied upon definite proof of ill-doing before assuming that a crime had been committed.
We have here section 10(1) (a), (b) and (c), which provide that anyone who fails to comply with the act or a regulation under it shall be guilty of an offence. We know how volatile are these regulations, and how heavy are the penalties imposed upon a person who has broken them. We are placing it within the power of an individual to make the law. and to change it without notice of any kind, and then we place upon the individual charged with its infraction the burden of proving his innocence. That is a drastic rule to apply at any time, even when the law is old and the people are well acquainted with it; but to apply that rule to legislation, passed in camera and arising out of an emergency, is so harsh as to imperil all respect for the law and to create ill-will and suspicion in the people as a whole.
I suggest to the minister-and I tell him that I have no confidence in the act itself- that he modify this severe and penalizing aspect of the act and that he treat any infraction of it as an ordinary infraction of the law is treated, and that he place upon him who lays the charge the full burden of proving intent to breach the law.

The remarks I made a few moments ago with respect to the burden of proof apply to section 12. I invite the members of the committee to look at section 12. In the first place, there is a burden on the crowm. The burden is this. The crown will have to prove, when a person is charged with an offence, that the person did an act for which a permit is required under this act. That is the burden of proof which the crown has to discharge. The crown having done that, then it is within the knowledge of the accused whether he has a permit or not; and I refer to the well recognized principles of British criminal law, that where the facts are peculiarly within the knowledge of the other party, and where the rule, if it were strictly followed, would require a .person to prove a negative, which is an exceedingly difficult thing to do, the burden can be shifted.
Under the administration of this particular act, where a man is charged with importing goods without a permit the crown will have to prove that he imported the goods; that they were goods of a category which required a permit, and it would be alleged that he did not have one. The burden would then, be shifted to the accused to show that, in fact, he did have a permit and that he did knowingly contravene a provision of the act. I think that is quite in conformity with a long line of statutes where circumstances are similar to this, and I do not think it is breaking new ground at all. I believe it is an entirely appropriate provision for a statute of this kind and I feel confident that it should remain in the statute.

I might express the view in passing that I do not see why opinions of the law officers of the crown, which are as important as this one is in purporting to find in favour of the government's power to proceed in this extraordinary way, should not be tabled in the house. It will be recalled that at the last session, when the opinion of the law officers of the crown was sought in connection with the wheat board matter, that opinion was given to the house by the present Minister of Justice, and certainly in a matter as important as this I do not think the house would be encroaching upon the realm of privileged communication between the law officers of the crown and the government in asking that a legal opinion, an opinion on a legal question whether there was power under the Foreign Exchange Control Act for the government to do what it has sought to do under order 4678, should be made available to the house.
However, to come back to this question, that opinion, giving full respect to the source of it -the law officers of the crown-was proceeded upon in breach of a solemn undertaking given to this house by the then minister of finance in the 1946 session when he introduced the Foreign Exchange Control Act in this house. Here was a solemn undertaking given to the house or, if you like, a representation made to the house by the then minister of finance, the present Minister of Justice, as reported1 at page 2547 of Hansard of 1946:
We have no intention of -using this exchange control legislation to restrict anything but certain types of capital movement.
What has been done under P.C. 4678 is to throw that undertaking or representation out of the window completely, to ignore it, a representation that was solemnly given to parliament, a representation that certainly entered into the consideration given that bill by many members. The committee will remember that the house spent some time on the bill when it was up in 1946. In the banking and commerce committee its sections were reviewed with some care, and that undertaking of the then minister of finance was an under-

taking upon which the banking and commerce committee and this house proceeded in their deliberations upon the bill. Had that undertaking not been given, I am sure the bill would have had a different reception both in this house and in the banking and commerce committee. And to my hon. friend the present Minister of Justice may I just say in passing that I find it very difficult to understand how he can submit to continuing to be a member of the present government when the present government has completely ignored and repudiated the solemn undertaking which he gave the house in the session of 1946.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend should be careful of his language. There was no solemn undertaking given by any minister of the crown.. My predecessor as minister of finance said, and I made a somewhat similar statement in the banking committee, that it was not the intention of the government to use the Foreign Exchange Control Act for the purpose of imposing import restrictions on imported goods. I dealt with it at some length in my broadcast address when announcing this policy and have done so subsequently. I may be criticized for it, but I take exception to the statement that the then minister of finance gave a solemn undertaking, because he did no such thing.

I wish to state quite as positively, if I may do so, that the statement I have quoted, given by the present Minister of Justice and then minister of finance, was a solemn statement given to the house. It was part of a prepared statement.

speechtext: I am saying that it was not a solemn undertaking. That is all.

And it was on the strength of that assurance, that the government would not use this legislation, the Foreign Exchange Control Act, to restrict certain types of capital movement, that the house proceeded to deal with the bill as it did. That assurance underlay all the deliberations of the house on that measure. It underlay all the deliberations of the banking and commerce committee on the measure. There can be no gainsaying that fact. It was an undertaking of the highest importance to the house and to the banking and commerce committee, and surely, when important legislation is introduced and well considered statements, prepared statements,
are submitted to the house by ministers speaking in the name of the government, statements containing assurances as plain and as solemn as that, this house is entitled to believe that the government will not repudiate such a promise or such an undertaking without first coming to the house. But there was nothing of that sort in this case. The government sent two ministers on the air, two ministers after the Prime Minister, to announce in effect that, regardless of this undertaking, regardless of this solemn assurance, the government, without coming to parliament and saying so much as "by your leave", would blindly go ahead and by order in council, in the face and the teeth of its undertakings, put into effect in peacetime the greatest restrictive program, the greatest measure of strangulation applied to our economy, ever imposed in time of peace.
The measure before us, Bill No. 3, would be bad enough under the best of circumstances. That the government should ask parliament to clothe it with powers so dictatorial, so vast, powers that can be so arbitrarily exercised, as the government in this bill is asking parliament to clothe it with, is bad enough. But when that measure follows by some months the putting into effect by the government of an order in council so drastic in its effect, and so completely in the teeth and in defiance of solemn government undertakings, I say, Mr. Chairman, that not only has a grave wrong been done to parliament, but there has been a complete slap in the face to all fundamental conceptions of democracy.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The reason why no time limit is put in this act is that, by its very nature-with prohibitions, quotas and a permit system; particularly schedules I and II relating to prohibitions and the quotas-if a definite time were fixed, or if it were thought that the act might expire at a certain definite time, obviously it would make for speculative opportunity on behalf of some people. It is almost in the nature of a budget change. It seems to me that certain sections of this bill need to be handled almost on the basis on which one makes changes in existing tariffs, and there should not be any possibility of anyone having any real advance notice as to when that is likely to take place. That is why no definite time is fixed in this act as to when it shall expire; and I think there are the most compelling reasons why there should not be any such time fixed.
I would point out that there is a definite time limitation in the Foreign Exchange Control Act, which I believe is March 31, 1949.

The procedure ever since I have been here has been to take them individually. I remind the committee that when we were on second reading of this bill we from this corner of the house indicated the precise reasons for our objections to the bill. One of the reasons which we indicated at that time was the government's unwillingness to reconsider its ban on fresh fruits and vegetables. The reply of the minister to that point when he concluded the debate on second reading was that it did not invalidate the principle; that it was only a detail which we could deal with when we got to committee.
Now that we have come to this detail in the committee, I hope that we shall deal with it fairly and objectively and not just have it pushed through. In fact, it seems to me that this item and also item No. 92 are items on which the government ought to permit a free vote of the committee. I point out, Mr. Chairman, that there are many items in the schedule which we in this group and other members of the committee might have sought to make an issue out of, but we accept the general principle that the government has to do something along the line of restricting imports to overcome our shortage of United States dollars. In other words, we are not going through the schedule and picking out item after item so as to upset the whole program; but we are picking out these two items, fresh fruits and fresh vegetables, because we believe they are important to the health of our people.
The minister has already today made remarks to the effect that we did not have these things in the wintertime in Canada twenty-five or fifty years ago. I submit that that answer is not good enough. The fact is that during the past quarter of a century, and especially during the last century, the age to which Canadians live has been extended, and it just may be that, in part, that is due to what we have learned about nutrition. No one will deny that from a nutritional point of view it is exceedingly important that we have fresh fruits and vegetables in this country, particularly so in view of the wintry climate that we have in Canada. I would suggest that we
Foreign Exchange Conservation

have no way of telling what injury we may do to the health of the Canadian people in years far distant by the action of this committee if the majority supports these two items and cuts down on the quantities of fresh fruits and vegetables that are available to our people. When I indicated a moment ago that we were prepared to make an issue out of these items, 87, 92 and 96, the minister gave me a figure as to what the total amount of these three items came to last year. I think he said $17,000,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Approximately $17,000,000 for out-of-season vegetables, not fruit.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I believe that the figures which the minister has given with regard to this whole program of import restrictions is something of the order of $300 million. I agree that if we were to go through the list and pick out item after item it would total $50 million, $100 million or $200 million, and we would then certainly be defeating the whole program of the government; but $17,000,000 does not upset the program that the government is trying to put through; and I submit it is more important that this committee concern itself with the health of our Canadian people. I know that I am speaking for hon. members in all parties, for all of us have received strong representations from individuals and from organizations back home. This is another of those occasions where I feel the government should permit a free vote of the committee. I am sure that if a free vote were permitted and hon. members voted the way they know the people back home wanted them to we would delete item 87. We would do the same thing with items 92 and 96 when we get to them. Mr. Chairman, I call upon the committee to vote down item 87.

May I ask the minister a question? Could not substantial quantities of the products mentioned in item 87 be brought in from	the	British	West Indies	and	other
countries?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am told not. We can get from	the	British	West Indies	and	other
countries fruits which are under schedule II, under the quota. There is no effective limitation at all. Onions come from Bermuda. These are quotas, and there is no effective limitation on the import of onions from Bermuda.
Tomatoes?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Tomatoes we have allowed in from the Bahamas under the special hardship clause. There are none available from the Bahamas because we have taken the crop.

What the situation may be next year it is hard to say. That is true of Montserrat and Jamaica.

I have listened to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. Like myself, he has been to Great Britain, and I understand that he is greatly in favour of the planned economy they have in that country. The last time I was there I never saw an orange; I never saw imported vegetables; I never saw the things one sees in vast quantities in Canada. And I speak not as an authority; I am repeating statements made by the Ministry of Food in Great Britain, when I say that the British people have never been healthier. I think that in a comparative sense it can be said that we are well off in Canada, and I do not think it is a great hardship, for a few weeks in the year, in order to protect our economy, for us to deny ourselves these things that we got along without, at any rate when I first came to this country, which is not very long ago. I think that is a fair statement to make. Comparatively speaking, the British people are in the same position as ourselves, for they are trying to protect their currency and they have found it necessary to deny themselves in this way for years, ever since the outbreak of the war; nevertheless the British people, it is said, are healthier today than they have ever been.

I come from the centre of one of the most important sections in Canada growing fruits and vegetables, and I want to suggest to my hon. friend who objects to this item that the amount involved in out-of-season fruits and vegetables-he is only giving half the picture-is closer to $40,000,000. I admit at once that, on account of the suddenness with which the emergency came upon us, our growers have been caught out of their stride, but I want to assure him that the Ontario and British Columbia fruit and vegetable growers will supply him and his family with all the fresh fruits and vegetables they can eat. It is true we are short of cabbages and celery and all these things now, but that is only because the emergency came upon the country in an out-of-crop season and there was no opportunity for the growers to prepare for it. You will have all the cabbages, carrots, beets, celery, spinach and all these other vegetables next winter, grown in Canada. I do not think anyone's health will suffer because we are denied strawberries three or four weeks ahead of time or denied asparagus three or four weeks ahead of time. Our asparagus is better than the United States asparagus, if you wait for it.

Foreign Exchange Conservation

British Columbia has been mentioned. I dio not think the . Fraser valley can supply any whitloof-I do not know what that is-and Saskatchewan may have to 'be denied watercress for a few weeks in the year.

The minister said the other day that carrots would 'be allowed1 in. I understand that in Ottawa they are in Short supply and tlhe minister's home town will be out of carrots this week. I agree in part with what the hon. member for Halton has said. This emergency was thrust upon the people of Canada, and if thie farmer had known three or four months before, he would have been able to supply the market. He should have been told. Even at the present time, the truck farmers do not know what the program is for next year, and they will not be able to supply the market unless they are informed at once so that they can buy the seed to plant this year; because, as the Minister of Agriculture will tell you, the seed is generally bought either in December or January, and it is getting late now to buy seed to supply the people of Canada with the fre^h vegetables they need. Fifteen years ago the farmers of Canada supplied enough vegetables to the people of Canada right until April. They were stored in their basements. We have rhubarb which is now imported, or was imported from the United1 States.
Nonsense.

Pardon me, it was, in the winter. But rhubarb for winter consumption was first grown in Canada, and first grown by the uncle of the hon. member for York East in Hamilton, Ontario, in his basement and shipped from Canada to New Y'ork. On the menus there it appeared as fresh rhubarb imported from Canada. I do not agree that this whole list of things should be cut off in item 87. There are some of these things we can do without; but what I am afraid of is that if this is wiped, out, when our own farmers are bringing in their crops next summer, or when, they are about ripe, the government will allow an influx, a flood of things from the United States, as they have done in the last few years.
Shame.

Yes. Strawberries have been mentioned. Strawberries have flooded this country just a few weeks before our own Canadian strawberries have gone on the market. They killed the appetite of the Canadian people for our own strawberries, and
our own producers were not able to get a proper price. If our own farmers are given proper protection we shall have enough vegetables in Canada, but they demand protection and should have it. I think the Minister of Agriculture should get together with *the Minister of Finance and state t'he policy in regard to vegetables, and state it at once.

With reference to the statement of the hon. member for Halton, that we can supply in this country a lot of these fresh fruits and vegetables which we are importing from the United States, I have asked a question two or three times in the house, and I suggest to the hon. gentleman that he put it to t'he government. Perhaps they will answer him, but they will not tell me. Can these growers in Canada be given an assurance that this program will not be limited and that the United States product will not come here and flood this market after our growers made a,n effort to produce t'he things we need? Will he ask the government that?

I have discussed the
problem thoroughly with our growers and I am told that there is no need at the present time for any such assurance. The growers will grow to the fullest extent of their capacity to take care of the Canadian public for the first part of the crop. We have two crop seasons; and so long as our growers have an assurance not later than the thirtieth of April, they will produce all the vegetables needed for the Canadian public next winter. I have already suggested to the minister that it would be in order to give such an assurance, and between now and the first of May you can rest assured that it will be repeated.
The first of May will, be too late.
No, it will not be too late.
The growers must start to make preparations.
They have to buy fertilizer and seed.
Our growers do not wait until Monday to buy the fertilizer they need on Tuesday.

It is not a question of waiting until Monday to buy fertilizer. We on Vancouver island are sowing vegetable seeds now, in the month of February. I appreciate the government's difficulty. I see their desire to save a considerable sum of money. I also appreciate the point of view put forward by the hon. member for Winni-
1336

Foreign Exchange Conservation
peg North Centre. The health of this country is threatened if the people cannot get sufficient fresh vegetables. Surely the answer is simple. Surely one of the ministers of the government can assure the vegetable growers of this country that for this growing season, whether the vegetables are sown in the month of February or in the month of May, they will be able to harvest their vegetables and supply the people of Canada without having unfair competition placed upon them by the sudden opening of the market to United States vegetables. I am certain-and I have discussed the matter with vegetable growers this year; in fact, I discussed it last Christmas-that they are prepared to make a considerable outlay of capital, bring more acreage under cultivation, invest in newer equipment, so that they can cultivate their vegetables in sufficient quantity to supply the people of Canada. They are prepared to do all that if they can be given some reasonable guarantee as to the security of their market. I ask for this year that the government, if they want to save that amount of money, at least assure the vegetable growers now that they will not be subjected to unfair competition at harvest time.

I had not intended to speak in this debate, even though I represent a rural district and have been a member of the committee on agriculture and colonization. Having listened to the hon. member for Nanaimo, I should like to know if it is possible for him to give us for all Canada, with the exception of Victoria and Vancouver island, a sort of formula by which it would be possible to bring in cucumbers, tomatoes and so on during the winter months.
Move to British Columbia.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I should like the Liberal members of the house to realize the position that the country is getting into under this whole program. The Minister of Finance has protested strongly against our claims that this whole bill was protectionist in nature. Once or twice he said it was the highest form of protection.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have not protested. I myself have said it was highly protectionist.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The minister said both things.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have not said both things. From the beginning I have said that it is highly protectionist.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: In answer to the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard, the minister said it was the highest form of protection. But to me, on second reading, the minister said that it was not intended to be protectionist; that it was intended to be restrictive.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right.
All things to all men.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: We have a proposal that these fresh vegetables be prohibited at the present time. The hon. member for Halton gets up and assures us-and I have no doubt he knows of the assurance that he is giving- that the vegetable grower's in his part of the country can step up their production to meet this changed situation. It means that a year or two from now, those vegetable growers, having built up their production-whether economic or otherwise-behind this highest form of protection, will be coming to the Liberal government and asking the Liberal government to keep this kind of protection in effect.
AVe shall still be in power.
Don't brag.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
The Liberal party may still be in power but its Liberalism will have vanished completely. The hon. member for Fraser Valley who, I think, believes to a considerable extent in free trade, will find it difficult to continue to support a government which not only has brought in the highest form of protection but finds itself in the position of having to keep that wall of protection there. It is the same old story that we have had throughout the whole history of Canada. I am talking to my Liberal friends now, not to the Tories. The Tories like this. It is the same old story of protection for an infant industry, and then the infant industry needs that protection for all time. In my view, there are many other ways in which this government has discriminated against the agricultural industry of this countiy that it must overcome. But this is not the way. This, in the long run, reduces the standard of living of the Canadian people; it reduces their purchasing power; and when the standard of living of the Canadian people goes down, the section of the community which suffers the must is the agricultural section. This course is completely "il-Liberal", and the demonstration we have had tonight shows that the minister's claim that this is just a temporary measure is just so much eyewash. It is the

Foreign Exchange Conservation
beginning of a wall of protection; and once you get it built up, the tendency is for the people who have enjoyed that protection to want it to be built still higher. I submit that that argument falls to the ground and that the argument with regard to the health of the Canadian people is the one which this committee should consider. I think we should vote down this section. I agree with those who have said that there are one or two things in it such as watercress, endives, eggplant and so on which, so far as I know, are not of particular importance from the point of view of health. But I can see the great difficulties that we might get into in this committee if we went through the twenty odd items and tried to make amendments to strike out a few of them. This section deals with the banning of fresh vegetables in general, and I think the members of this committee should take this opportunity to speak for their constituents and vote it down.
Oh, no.

I do not know how expert my hon. friend is, but my information comes from a man who handles these products, and I believe it is thoroughly reliable. Lettuce cannot be kept for more than two weeks. I also understand that the market gardeners of Canada would prefer that these fresh vegetables be allowed to come in during the winter months, because people develop habits in eating as in other things, and if they are able to get vegetables during the winter they will be likely to continue eating them during the summer. That is sound reasoning. Furthermore, it is sometimes difficult to get children to eat certain vegetables, and if they are away from them for four or five months out of the year it is hard to get them to eat them again.
May I now say something about the nutritional aspect, which was mentioned by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. We have heard some very offhand expressions about having done so well over the past twenty or thirty years, as far as nutrition is concerned, when we did not have these imported vegetables. That has been told us not only by the Minister of Finance but also by the Minister of Labour a moment ago. I am not at all certain that the people in Britain may not get fresh vegetables from some of the south European countries where the currencies are weakened. Certainly they have their Brussels sprouts; there is no doubt of that. In regard to the value of present-day diets, which we are not able to maintain because of these restrictions, I should like to read from the proceedings of the national nutrition conference for defence, held at Washington on May 26, 27 and 28, 1941. I refer to the concluding address by Thomas Parran, surgeon general of the United States public health service. This, I think, will establish that, while we existed, and not badly, in years gone by, we have greatly improved our standards. Surgeon General Parran says:
In the past two decades there have been breath-taking discoveries on many nutritional fronts. To find a parallel to this swift advance in knowledge we must go back to the epochmaking time of Pasteur, whose germ theory of

Foreign Exchange Conservation
disease made possible a half century of progress against preventable infections. Without Pasteur and his co-workers and disciples, mankind still would be plague-ridden. He made our civilization vastly different. Tomorrow's civilization can be made vastly different, and far better than today's, if we put to work now, what we know now, about the nutrition of human beings.
In the past half century we have added twenty years to the average span of human life-
I hope the Minister of Finance will remember that.
-largely by saving the lives of babies and of young people. But life expectancy for those of us beyond the age of forty has not increased since Pasteur's time. On the contrary, many .[DOT]diseases have increased because more of us grow old enough to acquire them. Deaths have increased from cancer, heart conditions, kidney conditions, mental illness-in fact, from all of the so-called degenerative causes. It is easy to say that this is the strain of modern life. Yet every disease, every malfunction of an organ, results from a derangement in the functioning of the individual body cell. The individual cell functions properly if it is properly fed; and if it is not killed by the invasion of bacterial, virus, or chemical poisons, or by endogenous toxins. The food available to each of the body cells probably determines to a large degree the health of that cell, its proper functioning, its reciprocal relations with other cells, which make up organs and systems of the body.
Then later:
Doctor Sherman has told us that if we replace an average diet-
Such as the Minister of Finance no doubt had, and under which he flourished so well.
-with an adequate diet wye get a ten per cent increase in the active, virile life span.
Some lion. MEMBERS: Hear, hear.

It is quite easy to see that I am good until at least eleven o'clock.
Schedule I stands.
Progress reported.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: As previously arranged, tomorrow we go back to the debate on the address. If we should complete that we shall return to the emergency legislation, this measure being first.
Would the Secretary of State for External Affairs say whether we shall continue with Bill No. 3 on Friday if the speech from the throne is not disposed of before that time?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That would be my intention, Mr. Speaker.
